Sheshai
SHEE-shy
n. (proper, one of the three sons of Anak)
Hebrew Sheshay, probably whitish or noble. He is named three times, always with his two brothers Ahiman and Talmai, and always in connection with Hebron.

Biblical Definition

The twelve spies met them: “And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)” (Numbers 13:22). Forty-five years later the same three are driven out by one man: “And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak” (Joshua 15:14). And at the opening of Judges the tribe finishes the work: “And Judah went against the Canaanites that dwelt in Hebron: (now the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba:) and they slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai” (Judges 1:10). Scripture names all three men in all three passages. The giants who made ten spies feel like grasshoppers are not left as a vague terror; they are named, counted, located and finally killed, and the record of their defeat is as specific as the record of the fear they caused.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the three sons of Anak who dwelt in Hebron and were driven out by Caleb.

expand to see more

ANAK, n. The progenitor of the Anakim, a race of giants in the hill country of Canaan.

GRASSHOPPER, n. An insect of the genus Gryllus; in Scripture, a figure of smallness and insignificance.

SPY, n. A person sent into an enemy's camp or country to inspect their works, ascertain their strength and designs.

TERROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind.

CONQUEST, n. The act of conquering; the act of overcoming or vanquishing opposition by force.

Key Scripture

Numbers 13:22 — "And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)"

Joshua 15:14 — "And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak."

Judges 1:10 — "And Judah went against the Canaanites that dwelt in Hebron: (now the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba:) and they slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai."

Numbers 13:33 — "And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight."

Modern Corruption

Fear works by keeping its objects vague and enormous; Scripture names the three giants, notes where they lived, and then records exactly who killed them and when.

expand to see more

Numbers 13:33 is the classic description of how fear distorts a report: And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight. Notice the last clause. The spies did not merely report the giants' size; they reported the giants' opinion of them, which no one had told them. Fear supplies the other side's thoughts and then treats the invention as intelligence. It is worth saying plainly because the habit is universal, and it kept a generation out of the land.

The corrective in the text is the naming. Ahiman, Sheshai, Talmai — three men, not a legend; living in Hebron, not everywhere; and in Joshua 15 driven out by an eighty-five-year-old, and in Judges 1 slain by Judah. Scripture keeps the same three names across three books so that the reader who trembled in Numbers can see the account closed. Bring a fear into the light, count it, name it and set it beside the promise of God, and it has already lost the part of its power that came from being vague.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Sheshay (H8344), whitish or noble; Achiyman (H289), Ahiman; Talmay (H8526), Talmai; chagab (H2284), a grasshopper.

expand to see more

Hebrew Sheshay (H8344) — Sheshai, one of the three sons of Anak at Hebron.

Hebrew Achiyman (H289) — Ahiman, brother of a gift; named with him in all three passages.

Hebrew Talmay (H8526) — Talmai, furrowed; the third brother.

Hebrew Nephiyl (H5303) — the giants, the fallen ones; the stock the spies reported.

Hebrew chagab (H2284) — a grasshopper; the spies' estimate of themselves.

Usage

"“Where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were”."

"“Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak” — one man, three giants."

"“They slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai” — the account closed."
